cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
Today we identify components and learn what their measured curves actually
mean.
For a junction diode's forward characteristic, connect a safe low voltage
source through a current limiting resistor and a series ammeter.
Measure voltage across the diode itself.
Forward bias means its anode is at higher potential than its cathode.
Start low and increase the setting gradually, taking paired diode voltage and
current readings within the component and meter ratings.
The series resistor limits current; it is not part of the voltage measured
across the diode.
Suppose two nearby original observations are zero point six five volts at two
milliamperes, and zero point six seven volts at four milliamperes.
At the second point, static resistance is zero point six seven divided by zero
point zero zero four, or one hundred sixty seven point five ohms.
But the local incremental resistance is the voltage change divided by the
current change: zero point zero two volts over zero point zero zero two
amperes, giving ten ohms.
These are different questions.
The first uses a line from the origin; the second describes the local curve
over a small interval.
The curve rises steeply rather than obeying one constant resistance.
There is no universal perfectly sharp zero point seven volt switch for every
silicon diode.
Temperature, device and current matter.
State your graph axes and units, allow for meter loading, and never connect a
diode directly across an unrestricted supply.
Reverse the diode orientation while keeping a suitable protective resistor and
a supervised low voltage source.
The cathode is now at higher potential than the anode.
With diode voltage defined as anode potential minus cathode potential, reverse
voltage is negative.
Define forward conventional current as positive, and the reverse current is
negative too.
The ordinary reverse branch therefore lies in the lower left quadrant on a
signed I V graph.
Some laboratory plots instead show positive reverse voltage and reverse
current
magnitudes.
Those plots are fine when clearly labeled, but do not silently mix the two
conventions.
Before breakdown, a real diode usually carries a small reverse leakage
current,
not an exactly zero current.
Choose an appropriately sensitive range, and recognize that voltmeter loading
can become significant when the current being measured is tiny.
A meter display of zero may mean below its resolution rather than no physical
current.
Suppose a signed observation is minus three volts and minus two microamperes.
Its current magnitude is two microamperes, or zero point zero zero two
milliamperes.
It is not two milliamperes.
At sufficiently large reverse voltage, breakdown can cause a strong current
increase.
An ordinary diode must not be deliberately pushed into breakdown unless the
device ratings and an approved protected procedure permit it.
A Zener device is designed for controlled reverse breakdown operation, but
even
it needs current limitation.
The JEE lesson here is interpreting polarity, quadrant and measurement scale
before reading the curve.
For a Zener reverse characteristic, the current remains small before the
breakdown region, then increases strongly while the diode voltage changes much
less.
A protected measurement can reveal that steep branch.
In our magnitude plot, both reverse voltage and reverse current are shown as
positive values, with the convention stated.
Never interpret nearly constant voltage as unlimited permissible current.
Suppose our ideal classroom circuit has a nine volt supply, a five point one
volt Zener operating in breakdown, and a three hundred ninety ohm series
resistor, with no parallel load.
The resistor drops three point nine volts.
Current is three point nine divided by three hundred ninety, giving ten
milliamperes.
The Zener dissipates five point one times zero point zero one watts, or fifty
one milliwatts.
The resistor dissipates current squared times resistance, or thirty nine
milliwatts.
These are model values; an actual design needs suitable ratings and margin.
Now imagine nearby measured points: five point zero eight volts at eight
milliamperes, and five point one two volts at twelve milliamperes.
The local dynamic resistance is zero point zero four volts over four
milliamperes, giving ten ohms.
The finite slope explains why voltage is not exactly constant.
A datasheet specifies breakdown at a test current and includes tolerance,
power
and temperature limits.
Do not identify the supply setting as the Zener voltage without measuring the
diode itself.
Use a stable source, protected connections and observations within the rated
range.
A mixed collection of components becomes manageable when you combine
appearance, markings and a safe electrical test.
A resistor often has two leads and color bands.
For a four band resistor, the first two bands are digits, the third is a
multiplier, and the fourth is tolerance.
Red, violet, brown and gold mean twenty seven times ten ohms, with five
percent
tolerance: two hundred seventy ohms.
Its nominal tolerance interval is two hundred fifty six point five to two
hundred eighty three point five ohms.
A capacitor also has two terminals, but stores charge rather than maintaining
a
steady ohmic current.
A common three digit code one zero four means ten times ten to the four
picofarads: one hundred thousand picofarads, or one hundred nanofarads.
Check the marking system rather than assuming every number follows that code.
Electrolytic capacitors are commonly polarized; their stripe often marks the
negative lead, but verify the actual part.
Safely discharge them through an appropriate resistor before testing, never by
a deliberate short circuit.
A diode's body band commonly marks the cathode.
In diode test mode an ordinary silicon junction typically gives a finite
forward drop and an over range indication in reverse, depending on meter and
device.
An LED emits light under suitable forward current, often has a different
forward drop, and may not light from every meter.
Lead length and a flat edge are clues, not guarantees on damaged or unfamiliar
parts.
Test isolated, unpowered components, and consult ratings before applying a
supply.
The identification requirement also includes transistors and integrated
circuits.
A typical bipolar transistor has three terminals: base, collector and emitter.
But a three lead package alone is not proof of a bipolar transistor; other
devices use similar packages.
Read the part number and check its datasheet.
In a simple unpowered diode test check, a silicon NPN transistor usually
behaves like two junctions sharing a base: a positive probe at the base and
negative probe at either emitter or collector gives a forward junction
reading.
Reversing those probes generally gives an over range reading.
For a PNP transistor, the corresponding conducting polarities reverse.
This is an identification model, not a full transistor performance test.
It does not reliably distinguish collector from emitter in every device, and
protection structures or a damaged part can change readings.
Confirm the actual pinout before connecting anything.
An integrated circuit contains several circuit elements in one package.
A dot or notch commonly indicates pin one orientation, and the part number
tells you which datasheet to consult.
You cannot determine every pin's role from the package outline.
Different integrated circuits may look almost identical while doing completely
different jobs.
Avoid powered resistance tests and static discharge into sensitive parts.
Before accepting an identification, combine at least two appropriate clues
rather than guessing from color or shape.
Our diagrams are representative teaching sketches, not universal component
pinouts.
These original examples conclude the introductory experimental skills set;
further observation tables, corrections and mixed JEE practice are still
needed.
Learning the laboratory principle is not a substitute for supervised hands on
work.
